newsitem.title: UK: Buyers rumoured in latest twist to UK Co-op saga.
newsitem.headline: Buyers rumoured in latest twist to UK Co-op saga.

text.p: Ireland's Allied Irish Banks and retailer J.Sainsbury might buy parts of Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society if an entrepreneur's bid for the group succeeds, newspapers said on Sunday.

Months of speculation came to a head on Friday when Andrew Regan's Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica confirmed that a group it co-owns had planned a bid for the CWS but that it had been temporarily thwarted by legal moves.

The Sunday Times said Allied Irish (AIB) would buy the and highly successful, CWS-owned Co-operative Bank Plc for between 350 and 400 million pounds ($652.9 million) if Galileo Group, a bidding vehicle, succeeded in its break-up attempt.
But the Sunday Telegraph reported that AIB would pay 220 million pounds for the bank, whose environmental and ethical banking stance resulted in pre-tax profits of 45.5 million pounds for 1996.
The Sunday Times said Sainsbury would join the bidding team with the aim of buying some of the larger CWS retail outlets in an expansion drive.
The AIB was not immediately available for comment on the report and a Sainsbury spokeswoman declined to comment on "speculation".

The latest reports followed a week of high drama for the 153-year-old CWS, whose interests range from supermarkets and travel agents to funeral parlours, farms, factories and a large insurance company, which the Sunday Telegraph said would be hived-off for up to 1.5 billion pounds.
It began with the CWS revealing a 10 million pound fall in pre-tax profits to 54.1 million pounds for the year to January 11 and ended in court action to prevent a bid for the mutually-owned group.

Galileo, widely believed to be backed by several big City institutions, had been expected to make a 1.0 and 1.5 billion pound bid for the Co-op after indications in February that it wanted to buy its non-food businesses for 500 million pounds.

After a phoney war lasting several months and fought largely on the pages of Britain's newspapers between Regan and the CWS, the battle heated up at the end of last week when the Co-op suspended two senior managers for an alleged breach of trust.

On Friday the group gained a court order preventing 31-year-old Regan, Lanica, Galileo, one of the CWS managers and a Regan advisor from using any confidential information they may have about the CWS.

It was later revealed CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth wrote to Hambros Bank, Regan's advisor on the bid, asking it to investigate what Melmoth described as "the suspicious nature of the circumstances" of a payment forming part of an earlier deal in which Regan bought a CWS food manufacturing arm.
Hambros officials were not immediately available for comment and while Regan's spokesman was also unobtainable, the Sunday Telegraph quoted Regan as saying he was unaware of impropriety.
A CWS spokesman confirmed that the group had hired a firm of private investigators to conduct surveillance on Regan, his advisor and the two CWS managers suspended last week.
"We had surveillance for a week and it stopped last Friday," he told Reuters.

CWS has already appointed investment bank SBC Warburg's Brian Keelan to mastermind its defence and city law firm Linklaters & Paines and accountants KPMG to conduct its own investigation into the affair.
Co-op insiders and analysts have said its complex structure and layers of individual and corporate membership should make any takeover attempt hard to execute.
But Galileo said on Friday it would first propose changing CWS to a public company at a special meeting. This would be followed by an offer to acquire the newly-created company.

While this could circumvent the Co-op's built-in defence mechanism, insiders have said throughout the saga that there was not enough support within the multi-billion pound organisation to give such a change the green light. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
